claims.text: A lightweight HEA based on Al, Cu, Ti, and V can provide a low-density starting material.
Standard casting and homogenization can produce a low-distortion initial state in the proposed lightweight HEA.
Room-temperature severe plastic deformation creates a high density of lattice distortions and subgrain boundaries.
Recovery annealing near 800°C relieves the lattice distortions introduced by severe plastic deformation.
The proposed comparison contrasts room-temperature SPD-treated specimens with recovery-annealed specimens under otherwise identical environmental tests.
Lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion and thereby increases mechanical strength.
Lattice distortions provide preferential nucleation sites for rapid oxide-scale formation.
Oxide scales nucleated at lattice distortions will be coherent and adherent.
A coherent protective oxide scale can improve corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Removing lattice distortions by recovery annealing diminishes both mechanical strengthening and accelerated protective-oxide formation.
Relative to the annealed baseline, SPD-treated samples will have higher yield strength.
Relative to the annealed baseline, SPD-treated samples will form a protective oxide scale faster and more uniformly.
SPD-treated samples will exhibit better corrosion resistance than the annealed baseline.
SPD-treated samples will exhibit better high-temperature oxidation resistance than the annealed baseline.
The hypothesized benefits cease after sufficiently prolonged annealing at about 800°C or above eliminates lattice distortions.
A critical density of lattice distortions is required to influence oxide-scale formation.
Existing evidence supports lattice distortion and pre-straining as contributors to mechanical strengthening.

Failure of the SPD-treated specimens to show statistically significant improvements in both strength and protective-scale-mediated environmental resistance would falsify the proposed dual-benefit mechanism.
